column5: GHA VIII (Mazrui, 1993) gives about 10,000 Algerian Muslim deaths for the Setif repression of 05/1945, a figure inside the course's range of 1,000 to 45,000 but stated without a method [CONTESTED]

Mazrui attributes the slogan 'seek ye first the political kingdom' to Nkrumah, notes that independence was necessary but not sufficient, and reads Nkrumah as meaning continental liberation; the course's wording matches. The 'all else will be subtracted' line is Mazrui's own gloss on Ghana and Uganda

Mazrui: Sharpeville (03/1960) taught that Gandhian civil disobedience could not succeed against entrenched white rule; the Angola rebellion followed about a year later and the Portuguese empire collapsed after the coup of 04/1974. Independence dates in Table 5.1: Ghana 06/03/1957, Guinea 02/10/1958, Nigeria 01/10/1960, Tanganyika 09/12/1961, Kenya 12/12/1963, Zambia 24/10/1964, Zimbabwe 18/04/1980, Namibia 21/03/1990

Mazrui lists five traditions of resistance (warrior, jihad, radical Christianity, non-violent mobilisation, guerrilla war); 87,000 Tanganyikans served with the Allies; Churchill and Roosevelt signed the Atlantic Charter in 08/1941; the UN Trusteeship Council lobbied against colonialism. These are an academic framing by one author in a UNESCO volume, not a consensus

GHA VIII Table 5.1 dates Algerian independence 03/07/1962 (the referendum result recognised by France); the course says 05/07/1962 (the day it was proclaimed and celebrated). Both dates are in use; state which one is meant

GHA VIII ch 24-25: 30 states were represented at the Addis Ababa conference opening 23/05/1963 and the Charter was signed on 25/05/1963; Togo (after Olympio's assassination) was not admitted and Morocco refused, and both signed later. So 30 at signing plus Togo and Morocco gives 32, which explains the 32 versus 33 counts in the course

GHA VIII calls Manchester 10/1945 the Fifth Pan-African Congress (over 200 participants, African delegates predominating, Nkrumah and Padmore joint secretaries, DuBois chair); the course's 'fifth' is right and Reader's 'sixth' is wrong

GHA VIII: First Conference of Independent African States, Accra 04/1958, eight states; the OAU set up the African Liberation Committee (nine states, HQ Dar es Salaam) with a voluntary Special Fund and declared 25 May African Liberation Day; the Charter lists seven principles, including territorial integrity of every state (not a pledge to keep colonial borders)

GHA VIII (Asante): sub-Saharan external debt rose from 6 to 32 billion dollars 1970-79 (from World Bank 1981); Africa grew 2 per cent a year in the 1960s against 4.1-7.2 per cent elsewhere; 16 of 25 least-developed countries were African in 1971; ECOWAS founded in Lagos 05/1975 with 16 members. Matches the course; Asante argues regional bodies depended on foreign donors and the Lome Convention

GHA VIII ch 10 (Chanaiwa, 1993): Sharpeville 21/03/1960, crowd of 10,000 to 20,000, police killed 72 and wounded 186 (40 women, 8 children); the course uses 69 official and at least 91 later, so this is a third figure from a general history without method. Soweto 1976: it says police killed 23 and wounded 200, an early count that is far below the course's 575 official to 02/1977; the chapter's date for the uprising is June to December 1976 [CONTESTED]

GHA VIII ch 10 slips and dates: it says the Group Areas Act of 1950 classified all South Africans by race (that was the Population Registration Act), writes 'Pan African Congress' for the Pan Africanist Congress, dates the Tomlinson Commission 1954 and 1956 in different places, but gives correct dates for Biko's death (12/09/1977), the PAC's founding (04/1959), the Treason Trial (156 accused, to 03/1961), the Defiance Campaign (8,500 arrested), the Portuguese coup (25/04/1974), the Lusaka Agreement (08/09/1974), the Rhodesian Internal Settlement (03/03/1978) and Zimbabwe's independence (18/04/1980). Use it for sequence, not for single numbers

GHA VIII ch 10: apartheid in 1948 as 'reincarnated Hitlerism' is Chanaiwa's rhetoric; migrant labour peak figures: South Africa about 600,000 and Southern Rhodesia about 250,000 migrants a year; the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland ran 1953-63; the Monckton Commission called partnership 'a sham'; Mondlane assassinated 02/1969; Cuban troops in Angola and the Namibia-Cuba linkage were settled in 1988-89 (Crocker, Gorbachev); the bantustan policy is called 'divide and rule' and the Transkei and KwaZulu leaders sought independence the state could not grant

GHA VIII ch 8 (M'Bokolo): the clashes of 11/1959 in Rwanda killed 200 to 270 with over 1,200 arrests and about 7,000 victims of destruction; the Gitarama coup of 28/01/1961 deposed the mwami and proclaimed the republic; local elections of 06-07/1960 gave Parmehutu 2,390 of 3,125 seats; Belgium, breaking with earlier policy, backed the Hutu; independence for Rwanda and Burundi came 01/07/1962. This puts a range of 200 to 270 beside HRW's 'several hundred'

GHA VIII ch 8: Belgian Congo: Leopoldville riots 4-7/01/1959, Brussels round table 01/1960 set independence for 30/06/1960, Lumumba founded the MNC in 10/1958 and was the only nationally based party leader, Kasavubu (ABAKO) represented regionalist and federalist views; Congolese in 1958 were 99 per cent of the population but controlled 5 per cent of capital investment. Cameroon: UPC 'bloody week' 22-30/05/1955, official dead 25 but five times that in fact; Um Nyobe killed in the 1957-58 pacification; Moumie killed in 1960. Angola 1961 repression: 30,000 to 50,000 dead and 150,000 to 200,000 in exile; independence 11/11/1975 (stated with Guinea-Bissau's 24/09/1973, which is why GHA IX's dates look muddled)

GHA VIII ch 9 (Twaddle): Mau Mau as a squatters' revolt, resistance to enforced agricultural policy, cultural revival, internal Kikuyu war and anti-colonial rising; fewer European civilians were killed than died in Nairobi traffic accidents in the period (supports the course's 32 settlers); emergency declared 10/1952 after Chief Waruhiu's murder; Operation Anvil 1954; KAU leaders were not the organisers (Kenyatta repudiated by the oath-takers); KANU won 67 per cent in the 1961 election and Kenyatta was released 08/1961; the British overestimated the military threat; the emergency ended after 1959 and Macleod's constitutional conference

GHA VIII ch 9: Tanganyika 12/1961 (TANU won 70 of 71 seats in 09/1960), Uganda 1962, Kenya 12/12/1963 after the 05/1963 election, Zanzibar independent 10/12/1963 then revolution 12/01/1964 and union as Tanzania 26/04/1964, Malawi 07/1964, Zambia 10/1964. Nyasaland emergency 1959: Devlin found 52 Africans killed, mostly by government action, and called the colony 'a police state'; Madagascar's 1947 rising of 29/03/1947 left 'close to 100,000' dead by the High Commissioner's figure in 1949 (the chapter does not endorse it); the chapter says Tanganyika's speed owed to Nyerere, TANU's cohesion and UN trusteeship

column4: Chapter 14, search for a new order
column5: Adedeji (ECA) traces the road to the Lagos Plan: ECA strategy 02/1971, OAU declaration 05/1973, ECA Revised Framework 1976, Monrovia Strategy adopted by OAU heads 07/1979; he calls the Plan Africa's economic Magna Carta and says it puts the domestic and regional market, not export earnings, at the centre. Insider account, advocacy not evaluation.

Oil price announced 23/12/1973 rose from US$5.04 to US$11.65 a barrel; Adedeji says it hurt oil-importing African states and the OPEC example did not carry over to other commodities, so the NIEO push (seven issues incl. debt, commodity stabilisation, 0.7 per cent aid) produced no result for Africa.

Mazrui section: Nyerere, elected OAU chairman 11/1984, named development, debt and drought as Africa's concerns and said debtors under-used the threat of default; African debts were modest beside Latin America's. Opinion of the authors; no figures given.

Chapter 14 is policy advocacy by an ECA insider (Adedeji, with Mazrui section); its statistics on manufacturing share (7.6 per cent of GDP at independence), export versus food growth and nationalisations are tables garbled in the text, so only the prose figures are usable.

Elaigwu argues independence leaders kept the colonial state intact: bureaucracy grew and kept colonial goals, Francophone states stayed in the franc zone, Nigeria left the sterling zone only in 1973. Kenyatta dismantled the majimbo regions by 1964 and Mboya rejected the Westminster model in parliament; Ghana became unitary under Nkrumah.

By the mid-1980s Africa had had more than 70 military coups (his Table 15.1, updated by UNESCO 1992), starting from Egypt 1952; he groups causes as societal, military, international and miscellaneous and calls military regimes better at state-building than nation-building.

Elaigwu says single-party states did better at national unity than multi-party ones, but admits Mali, Upper Volta and Nkrumah's Ghana were still overthrown; an arguable thesis from a 1993 volume, not a settled finding [CONTESTED].
A footnote calls Sekou Toure the grandson of Samori Toure; this is a family claim repeated by Toure himself and is treated with caution by historians. Not repeated in the course.
Banjul (African) Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights adopted 06/1981, in force 21/10/1986 once ratified by a majority, matching the course.

Kodjo and Chanaiwa: OAU diplomacy won UN recognition of the liberation struggle (General Assembly Resolution 2555), non-recognition of Smith's UDI, a UN Commission for Namibia, a Security Council meeting in Addis Ababa 28/01 to 04/02/1972, the Lusaka Manifesto (14 to 16/04/1969, presented to the UN by Ahidjo) and a Paris sanctions conference 20 to 27/05/1981 (122 governments) whose call for mandatory sanctions the Security Council refused.

OAU recognition was decisive for FRELIMO, MPLA, SWAPO, ANC and PAC; OAU pressure produced FRELIMO (from MANU and UDENAMO) and the Patriotic Front (ZANU and ZAPU); it denounced Tshombe and Savimbi. The authors rate 1963 to 1973 as organisation and manifestos with no concrete results, and 1973 to 1980 as the most fruitful decade. Authors' judgement.

The chapter says the Comoros, Seychelles and Zimbabwe all became independent in 1980; the volume's own Table 15.1 gives the Comoros 1975, Seychelles 1976 and Zimbabwe 1980, so only Zimbabwe fits. Another independence-date slip within the volume.

Chapter 25 says the African Charter was adopted at the Nairobi summit in July 1981 and has 67 articles; chapter 15 says June 1981. The summit was in late 06/1981 and the charter has 68 articles [check current]. Course does not mention the Charter; no change made.

Authors say the Algerian war split the continent: the Casablanca group backed Algeria's government in exile, with non-Arab members Ghana, Guinea and Mali, while the conservative Monrovia group leaned to France; the split was moderated after Algerian independence in 1962 and the OAU in 1963. Matches the course's two-group account.

Argues independence kept Africa in a Western orbit: states kept colonial-era agreements and defence pacts, and Guinea was cut off by France after 1958 until relations resumed in 1963. His list of Western interventions includes Kenya and Tanganyika 1964, the Shaba operations 1977 and 1978-9, and the Ghana coup of 1966, which he treats as Western-made. Polemical thesis; the Ghana and Congo claims are contested [CONTESTED]. Only the first ten pages of this chapter are in the file.

Coquery-Vidrovitch's World Bank table for low-income Africa: debt to GNP rose from 17.5 per cent in 1970 to 54.5 per cent in 1984; debt to exports from 75.2 to 278.1 per cent; debt service ratio from 6.1 to 19.9 per cent. Prose: share of export earnings paid in debt service rose from 18 per cent in 1980 to 26 per cent in 1982 (38 per cent for the poorest); public savings fell from 15 to 6 per cent of GDP; GNP per head fell about 3 per cent in 1985.

Africa took only 3 per cent of world direct foreign investment 1965 to 1983 (table: 0.2 bn dollars a year in 1965-9 to 1.4 bn in 1980-3); a World Bank hypothesis needed 35.2 billion dollars a year of external resources for modest growth, with a 1.5 billion shortfall in 1985. Kodjo told the OAU in Lagos in 04/1980: Africa is dying.

Post-war living standards fell, unrest followed: Thiaroye 1944, Douala 1945, Constantine 1945, Madagascar 1947, strikes in Abidjan and Dakar, the Rand miners 1946. France created the colonial franc in 1946 (1.70 French francs, 2 from 1948) and FIDES in 1946; Britain's 1940 Colonial Development and Welfare Act began at 50 million pounds over ten years, 120 million by 1945.

She argues French business accepted decolonisation after the 1951-2 recession because colonial profits (SCOA) were falling, so economic decolonisation preceded political decolonisation; Treaty of Rome 1957 associated the colonies with the EEC (Yaounde 1963 and 1969, Lome 1975, 1980, 1986; STABEX 1975). An interpretation by one author, not a settled finding [CONTESTED].

Says the 1937 Munich Agreement between Hitler and Mussolini ceded North Africa to Mussolini; the Munich Agreement was signed on 29-30/09/1938 and concerned Czechoslovakia. A dating and naming slip in the volume.

Wartime and post-war unrest turned trade unions from inter-racial class consciousness into nationalist protest; the chapter also gives rural-urban figures (Africa 219m to 560m people 1950-1980, urban 32m to 133m). Context, not repeated.
Boahen and Suret-Canale fix Ghana's independence on 5 March 1957; it came on 6 March 1957 (course already gives 06/03/1957). Another date slip in the volume.

The chapter's opening says the last two West African colonies became independent in 1973 and 1974, but Cape Verde became independent on 05/07/1975; only Guinea-Bissau (declared 24/09/1973, recognised 1974) fits.

Brazzaville conference 30/01 to 08/02/1944 ruled out self-government; first 1945 college had 117,000 voters out of 16 million in French West Africa; laws of 11/04/1946 (forced labour abolished) and 07/05/1946 (citizenship); RDA founded at Bamako in 10/1946; Cote d'Ivoire repression 1949-50 led Houphouet-Boigny to break with the communists in 1950; loi-cadre 1956-7; referendum 28/09/1958 with Guinea voting over 80 per cent no; Mali Federation independent 20/06/1960 and the others in 08/1960; Togo 27/04/1960.

Boahen argues the British reacted to nationalist pressure rather than running a plan (Hailey 1942, Colonial Office minutes), so initiative lay with West Africans, against Flint, Pearce and Fieldhouse; Ghana first because its parties agreed on date and constitution while Nigeria and Sierra Leone had regional parties; 100 killed in Sierra Leone 1955-6. A one-sided reading of a debated question [CONTESTED].

PAIGC founded in Bissau by Cabral and five companions (chapter gives 19/10/1956; usually given as 19/09/1956); dock strike August 1959 left more than 50 dead; armed struggle from 1963; Portuguese troops rose from 1,000 in 1961 to over 30,000 in 1967 while PAIGC held two thirds of Guinea; Cabral killed 01/1973; independence declared 24/09/1973; Salazar regime fell 04/1974.

Manchester congress is called epoch-making: Africans (Nkrumah, Awolowo, Kenyatta, Banda) played leading roles, it called for complete independence, strikes and boycotts, and no Africans from French, Portuguese or Belgian territories attended. Matches the course's turning-point account.

Tubman's Liberia (iron ore 112m dollars against rubber 30m in 1966; coup 12-13/04/1980) and the cultural and union sections (UGTAN 01/1957, Presence Africaine 1947) are not covered by the course; recorded only.

Ki-Zerbo, Mazrui and Wondji, citing Ranger: TANU saw itself as heir to Maji Maji (Nyerere: the nation was built on its ashes), Zimbabwean nationalists revived Chimurenga from 1896-7 and Mandela invoked the ancestors' wars. Nationalist readings of older resistance, which later work qualifies [CONTESTED]. The chapter dates Maji Maji 1904-6 in one place and 1905-7 in another; the course uses 1905 to 1907.

Pan-African leadership passed from the diaspora to Africa at Manchester (fifth congress, 1945); after Ghana's independence Nkrumah held two Accra conferences in 1958 (independent states and the All-African People's Conference), and pan-Africanism split into trans-Saharan (territorial) and trans-Atlantic (racial) strands, of liberation and of integration. Matches the course.

Five post-colonial regime types: socialist, military, apartheid, conservative, and liberal-pluralist (only the Gambia, Botswana, Senegal, Namibia and Mauritius); socialism failed, the authors say, because ethnicity beats class, elites were Westernised, collectivism rested on custom not command and economies stayed tied to the world market; Nyerere argued multi-partyism was a luxury Africa could not afford; the case for the one-party state had failed by the 1970s; multi-party demands returned in 1990. The authors' framework.

Says Sekou Toure, Modibo Keita and Nyerere made one-party states in the 1950s (and prints Madeira Keita); these came in the 1960s (Tanzania 1965, Mali 1960, Guinea 1958-60); Mwakenya is placed in the 1970s but belongs to the 1980s. Slips; not repeated.
Chapter 17 begins at the end of this file (Tshibangu on religion, to p. 507); it is not used by the course and is recorded here only as unread beyond the opening pages.

Title page: volume VIII, Africa since 1935, ed. Ali A. Mazrui with C. Wondji, first published 1993 by UNESCO with Heinemann and University of California Press; the committee had 39 members, two thirds African. Settles the volume's publication year at 1993; the contents page gives chapter titles and pages used to cite it.

Mazrui calls the Biafra war a world war in microcosm: French support for Biafra against British support for federal Nigeria; Israeli support for Biafra against Egyptian pilots for the federal side; South African and Rhodesian backing for Biafra; Chinese support for Biafra against Soviet backing for Nigeria, with Czech Delfin jets (banned May 1968, resumed after the Warsaw Pact invasion in 08/1968). Uli airport was its last frontier. Some of these alignments are asserted without sources [CONTESTED].

Mazrui reads the early OAU as shallow in depth but continental in width (Arab and black states); radical Casablanca stood for continental unity and against sub-regional integration, moderate Monrovia for sub-regional steps. Nkrumah's fall (02/1966) and Arusha (1967) shifted the divide; Ethiopia 1974, Lisbon 1974 and Angola moved the OAU left; Olympio's killing in Togo, early 1963, is called the first killing of a head of state and the coup after it the first south of the Sahara.

Work on the volume was completed in 1989, so it does not reflect later changes: the Namibian and South African transitions, the end of the Soviet bloc. Mazrui's introduction forecasts a racial war in South Africa and a nuclear-armed black South Africa, which did not happen. Dating caveat for every claim taken from this volume.

Women in the struggle (Hawa Ismen Ali, Dulcie September killed in Paris 03/1988, Angie Brooks UN General Assembly president 1969); Algeria's war ending the Fourth Republic in 1958 and Portugal's wars ending fascism in 04/1974; Nigeria 3 of 6 heads of government killed by 1979. Context, not repeated.

North Africa gave 216,000 men to 1940 including 123,000 Algerians, and 385,000 from 1943 to 1945 including 290,000 Algerians, Tunisians and Moroccans, to liberate France. Ferhat Abbas issued the Manifesto of the Algerian People (second version 31/03/1943) and Messali Hadj's party was banned 26/09/1939. Setif 8 May 1945 is described only as bloody incidents with a large number of deaths and no figure; the Algerian Statute of 20/09/1947 left control with the European minority.

Dates the first edition of the Manifesto of the Algerian People 10 February 1945, but the next sentence puts the second version on 31 March 1943; the first edition was 10/02/1943. A misprint within the chapter.

The Istiqlal manifesto of 11/01/1944 demanded independence and led to at least forty dead and a hundred injured by 02/1944; Bey Moncef of Tunis named a ministry without the resident-general in 1942 and was deposed 14/05/1943; Tunisian general strike at Sfax 28/06/1946. Context for the independence paths; not repeated.

Long sections on the 1930s slump, mining and farm prices, demography and shanty-towns in North Africa and the Horn, and on Egypt's 1936 treaty, Libya, Sudan and the Italian conquest of Ethiopia in 1935-6 (400,000 troops, Addis Ababa fell 1936). Not covered by the course.

Diop and others agree with the course: the Brazzaville conference of 01 to 02/1944 excluded any idea of autonomy or self-government, had no African delegates, and was presided over by Pleven; its impact has been much exaggerated, and its principles later obstructed French understanding of decolonisation. Also gives tirailleur numbers: 15,000 a year after 1930, 80,000 sent to France in 1939-40 and another 100,000 from 1943 to 1945.

French commandants de cercle ruled as despots, forced labour in Guinea (1,105 workers from one circle), Africans paid 2.6 francs per kg for cocoa against 4.5 for Europeans; Aline Sitoe's Joola revolt in 1942; Thies railway strike 1938 (six strikers killed, 53 wounded); Portuguese and Spanish rule harsher under Salazar and Franco; Mouridism and Hamallism. Context on the late colonial economy; not repeated.

Crowder places colonies on a spectrum: settler colonies (Southern Rhodesia: settlers held 49 million acres, over 50 per cent of the land by 1934, under the Land Apportionment Act 1930 and Natives Registration Act 1936), African-producer colonies (British West Africa) and company colonies (the Congo, where chefferies were cut from 6,095 in 1917 to 1,212 in 1938 and the Union miniere supplied nearly a third of state revenue). Belgian rule was labelled indirect but was supervised closely, like French rule; even Nigerian indirect rule was closely supervised (Abba's Gombe study).

Groundnut prices fell from 8 pounds 18 shillings a ton in 1929-30 to 2 pounds 13 shillings in 1933-4; copper fell 60 per cent 1930-2 and over 125,000 Congolese wage labourers lost jobs; Northern Nigerian farmers paid up to 70 per cent of cash income in tax; the 1937 Gold Coast cocoa hold-up. In war the Congo's tin output rose from 2,750 tonnes (1939) to 17,300 (1945), obligatory labour rose from 60 to 120 days a year by 1944, a 1941 Union miniere strike left seventy dead, and the Congo gave the Belgian government-in-exile 85 per cent of its funds and supplied uranium.

Crowder blames the 'fiasco of Congolese independence' on Belgium giving Africans little more than primary education and no political role until very late; in 1935 Belgium thought in terms of at least a hundred years, Britain of three generations, and a 1945 Colonial Office memo thought Gold Coast independence 'unlikely in much less than a generation'. Authors' judgement, but the dates are firm.

Debate whether the Depression or the war was the turning point for decolonisation; Sobhuza, Tshekedi Khama and recruitment; Colonial Development and Welfare Act of 1940 at 5 million pounds a year for the whole empire. Context.

Hrbek: nine historic chiefs launched the revolt on 01/11/1954 with 2,000 to 3,000 ALN men; French forces rose from 56,000 to half a million by 1960 while the ALN reached 130,000; Soummam congress 08/1956; GPRA formed 09/1958; Constantine plan 1958; referendum 01/07/1962 gave 99.7 per cent for independence; about half a million Europeans left by end of 07/1962 and under 20 per cent stayed. He says nearly one million Algerians died and two million were uprooted, a figure matching the official claim that most historians reject [CONTESTED].

Chapter says the FLN was founded in 05/1955 (it announced itself on 01/11/1954), Israel crossed into Sinai on 24/10/1956 (29/10/1956; 24/10 was the Sevres meeting), the Arab League intervention in Palestine failed by 'the end of 1978' (1948), and Djibouti became independent on 26/06/1977 (27/06/1977) [check current].

Free Officers took power 23/07/1952; Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal Company on 26/07/1956; Britain and France landed at Port Said 05/11/1956 and stopped at midnight on 06/11 under US and Soviet pressure; Hrbek treats it as a failure of gunboat diplomacy that made Nasser a symbol. Partisan wording in places (calls Zionism colonisation backed by imperial powers).

Sudan independent 01/01/1956 after the Equatoria Corps revolt of 08/1955, blamed on British separation of north and south and northern haste with Arabic; Libya independent 24/12/1951 as a federation under Idris, oil from 1959-60; Eritrea federated with Ethiopia 1950-2 and annexed 1962; British Somaliland independent 26/06/1960 and Somalia 01/07/1960; Djibouti 1977. Ethiopia's war losses given as over 760,000 dead.

Owusu: marketing boards and export taxes withheld at least 700 million pounds from producers between 1940 and 1962, one third to one half of output value; Ghana's co-operatives handled only 2.2 per cent of the 1939-40 cocoa crop while 13 expatriate firms controlled nearly 98 per cent; Tanzania's agencies paid farmers one fifth to one half of world cereal prices 1971-6 (Bates); urban food subsidies and overvalued exchange rates cut farm incomes and fed smuggling, as with Ghana's cocoa to Cote d'Ivoire and Togo.

Agricultural output growth fell from 2.7 per cent a year in the 1960s to 1.3 per cent in the 1970s, and per capita from plus 0.2 to minus 1.4 (food per capita minus 1.1) (FAO table); commodity terms of trade fell from 126 in 1953 to 86 in 1971; Ghana's cocoa earnings fell from 85.5 million pounds in 1954-5 to 77 million in 1964-5 although the crop rose from 210,000 to 590,000 tonnes; refugees rose from 750,000 to over 5 million in the 1970s.

By 1935 Africa produced 65 per cent of colonial palm oil, 63 per cent of groundnuts and 88 per cent of cocoa (1937 Chatham House table); roads and rail were built to export crops from near the coast, with a quarter of tropical African exports coming from within 161 km of it in 1957. Supports the course's colonial-economy account.
Settlement schemes (Gezira, the East African groundnut scheme of 1946, ujamaa), ecology, tsetse, drought and class sections; two cross-reference slips (table numbers) in the text. Context not used.

Kipre: colonial powers all avoided competing with home industry, so Africa's manufacturing stayed light; Africa produced only 0.9 per cent of world manufactured goods in 1980; imports of manufactures were over 60 per cent of imports in 1978; Nkrumah's plans put 72 per cent of 1959-63 and 61 per cent of 1964-70 budget credits into industry, with a public sector 10 to 12 per cent of industrial output by 1965 that did not survive 1966; Cote d'Ivoire's 1959 investment code favoured foreign capital; 67 per cent of approved 1965-70 investment in French-speaking Africa went to mining. Agrees with Adedeji's 0.9 per cent.

Urban population rose from 31.8 million in 1950 to 49.5 million in 1960 and 132.9 million in 1980 (4.8 per cent a year), driven by rural crisis more than by factory jobs; shanty-towns appeared from the 1930s (bidonville first used in Tunis in 1931); Mathare Valley in Nairobi and informal-sector survival. Matches Coquery-Vidrovitch's 32 to 133 million.

Egyptian, Liberian and South African industrial policy before 1960, Belgian Congo consumer industry rising from 30 to 44 per cent of the local market 1950 to 1958, and French industrial investment shares. Context not used.

Tshibangu on religion and social change: indigenisation of the churches, Islam's gains under colonial rule, independent churches (about 10,000 and 33 million faithful in 1987 per Barrett; Kimbanguist church about three million). Not covered by the course; nothing repeated. Also Sow and Abdulaziz open the language chapter (assimilation to 1960).

Sow and Abdulaziz: colonial assimilation to 1960, UNESCO's 1962 adult-literacy decision for African languages, centres at Niamey, Yaounde and Zanzibar, and a plea for language policy before 2000. Not covered by the course; nothing repeated.

Mazrui quotes Achebe on the black writer's duty to challenge injustice 'even against ourselves' in independent Africa; says the war produced little heroic writing because most post-colonial wars were civil wars, and that Christopher Okigbo's death (Mazrui wrote his only novel in response) drew a bigger literary response than 'half a million anonymous young Igbo'; names Anthills of the Savannah (1987) as Achebe's first novel since the war and Soyinka's The Man Died as an indictment of Gowon's detention.

Nyerere translated The Merchant of Venice and Julius Caesar into Kiswahili, which provoked a Tanzanian debate on whether blank verse is admissible in Swahili poetry; Mazrui reads the translations as part of the ujamaa vision (Mabepari wa Venisi, capitalists of Venice) and as promoting Kiswahili for world culture. Mazrui's own interpretation.

Seven literary conflicts (past and present, tradition and modernity, indigenous and foreign, individual and society, socialism and capitalism, development and self-reliance, Africanity and humanity); poetry and politics (Somali, negritude, Neto, Senghor); politicians quoting Shakespeare, Kipling and Tennyson (Awolowo, Mboya, Nkrumah). Context; Nobel prizes Soyinka 1986 and Mahfouz 1988 as stated.

Vansina on the visual arts, dress (Nkrumah's 1957 national dress, Mobutu's abacost), music (rumba, highlife, Fela), dance, theatre, cinema and television, with the view that the new arts date from the age of nationalist expectation (1945 to 1965), not from 1960. Not covered by the course; nothing repeated. The chapter's last pages begin the philosophy and science chapter (colonial disruption of African science).

Mazrui and Ajayi say Adedeji and the ECA stressed global constraints on Africa's development while the World Bank and IMF stressed mismanagement and policy errors; the ECA and OAU provided the economic analysis for the Lagos Plan of Action (1980), which they call an alternative paradigm to the World Bank's Berg Report. Supports the course's pairing of the two documents.
Dates the Berg Report to 1979; the World Bank's Accelerated Development in Sub-Saharan Africa was published in 1981 (the course gives 1981). Another dating slip [check current].
Records that Sudan's Nimeiri executed the theologian Mahmoud Muhammad Taha for apostasy in 1985 (01/1985), and Nimeiri was overthrown in 1985. Not used in the course.

Mazrui and Ajayi on colonial inhibition of science, Africa's minerals feeding Western industry (up to 90 per cent of cobalt reserves, in Zaire), UNEP's Nairobi base, nuclear research in Zaire and Ghana, three philosophical currents (cultural, ideological, critical), Nkrumah's gloriana, Nyerere as the most enterprising political philosopher; pre-Columbian African crossing claims (Bakari II, Van Sertima) are hedged by the authors as possibly romance [CONTESTED]; no African Nobel in the natural sciences. Largely outside the course; nothing repeated.

column4: Chapter 22 end and 23 opening, road to Manchester
column5: Harris: Italy's invasion of Ethiopia stirred pan-Africanism in the diaspora; C.L.R. James founded the International African Friends of Ethiopia in 1936 and the International African Service Bureau followed in 1937; Ras Makonnen's Manchester businesses were a base; the Pan-African Federation was formed in 1944 by Padmore, Kenyatta, Abrahams, Wallace-Johnson, James and later Nkrumah and organised the Fifth Congress at Manchester in 1945. Supports the course's account of Manchester as a turning point.

Habte and Wagaw: Addis Ababa education conference 05/1961 set targets 100:30:20 by 1980 from a 1960 base of 40:3:0.5; primary enrolment reached 62 per cent by 1980; higher education rose from 140,000 in 1960 to 1,169,000 in 1980; Nyerere's Education for Self-reliance. Not covered by the course; nothing repeated. Chapter 23 opens with the diaspora (brain drain, 450,000 Algerians in France during the war).

Asante: Casablanca group of 1961 was Ghana, Guinea, Egypt, Mali, Morocco, Libya and Algeria's government in exile; Monrovia group the other former French colonies plus Nigeria, Ethiopia, Liberia and Sierra Leone; 30 heads of state signed the OAU Charter on 25/05/1963; independent states rose from 9 to 26 in 1960 and 33 by 1964. Matches the course; the East African Community collapsed by 06/1977.

Chinweizu: UN Declaration for a New International Economic Order and Charter of Economic Rights and Duties of States (1974); UNCTAD IV (Nairobi, 1976) Integrated Programme for Commodities; the proposed Common Fund fell from 44 billion dollars to 10 billion with 1 billion paid up by 1983, and commodity agreements covered only five commodities by 1984; Lome I (1975, 9 EEC and 46 ACP), Lome II (1979, 58 ACP) and Lome III (1984, 64 ACP, 43 African) with STABEX for 34 then 44 commodities. African trade rose from 4.9 billion dollars in 1960 to 89.6 billion in 1980 with Western Europe still the main partner.

He argues Africa's failure rested on elites with a 'dependency mentality' who treated development as imported consumption (Nigeria's oil income dissipated abroad) and not only on external structures; calls blaming the West 'African irresponsibility' and notes Singapore, Taiwan and South Korea developed within the system. A polemical thesis against Rodney-style structural readings [CONTESTED]. Lonrho took 1.2 billion dollars of 4.7 billion revenue from Africa in 1982; Mozambique's GNP per head fell from 208 to under 155 dollars 1981 to 1983.
Chapter 26 dates Lome II to 1979 and Lome III to 1984, which is right; Coquery-Vidrovitch's chapter 11 gives 1980 and 1986 for them. An inconsistency between two chapters of the same volume.

Chinweizu's South Africa forecasts (capitalism may outlast apartheid) and Thiam and Mulira's opening on Soviet and Chinese policy: Lenin's pledge, Comintern links, Kenyatta's visits, 37 African countries with Soviet agreements 1957 to 1985, about 30,000 Africans trained in the USSR, China's 450 million dollar TAZARA railway. Context; not used.

column4: Chapter 27, Soviet aid to the Derg
column5: Thiam and Mulira: Ethiopia was the leading African recipient of Soviet military aid apart from Egypt: about 1 billion dollars of arms and 1,500 Soviet advisers and an estimated 20,000 Cuban troops during the Ogaden war, 1.5 billion in military aid by 1981, 3,500 students in socialist countries in 1979; they say Mengistu chose the socialist model partly to unify Ethiopia and that the Soviet Union also armed Somalia (181 million in military aid in 1977). Soviet-bloc sources and estimates are cited without audit.

USSR signed agreements with about 37 African countries 1957 to 1985 and trained some 30,000 Africans; China's TAZARA railway (1,278 miles, completed 1975, 15,000 Chinese and 30,000 African workers, cost 456.3 million dollars shared) and the Chinese–Soviet rivalry (China backed ZANU, USSR ZAPU); the 1988 Angola-Cuba-South Africa accords linked Cuban withdrawal to Namibian independence and owed something to perestroika. Mostly outside the course.

Socialist aid terms (2.5 to 3 per cent interest, 12 years), decline of Soviet influence in Guinea, Ghana, Mali, Kenya; chapter 28 opens with Africa's share of the UN (3 members in 1945, 50 in 1980) and Third World solidarity from Bandung 1955. Context; chapter 28 continues in the last file.

Edmondson: Cuba sent 18,000 to 24,000 combat troops to Angola in 1975-6, about 20,000 to Ethiopia in 1977-8, and at the 1978 peak had about 19,000 in Angola, 16,000 to 17,000 in Ethiopia and 2,455 to 2,755 advisers in 11 other states; Cuba chaired the Non-Aligned Movement 1979-82. Estimates from one cited study.

After the 1967 war only Guinea broke with Israel; in 10/1973 seventeen sub-Saharan states broke relations and four more followed in 11/1973, leaving only Malawi, Lesotho, Swaziland and Mauritius with ties; Edmondson rejects the idea that the oil weapon caused it. First Arab-African summit Cairo 07 to 09/03/1977 with 59 states. The text misprints October 1983 for October 1973.

The phrase New International Economic Order first appeared in the Algiers Non-Aligned economic declaration of 09/1973; the UN General Assembly's sixth special session (04/05/1974) adopted the Declaration and Action Programme and the Charter of Economic Rights and Duties of States passed on 12/12/1974 by 120 votes to 6 with 10 abstentions; UNCTAD began 1964 and the Group of 77 grew from 77 to 122 by 1980. Confirms the Adedeji and Chinweizu accounts.

Kouassi: the UN's Congo force arrived 15/07/1960 (300 Tunisians and 80 Ghanaians; 11,155 men by end of 07/1960); Hammarskjold accepted Tshombe's conditions at Elisabethville on 12/08/1960; Kasavubu dismissed Lumumba on 05/09/1960 and the UN's Cordier closed the radio station and Lumumba's villa was ringed by UN troops; Lumumba was killed in Katanga on 17/01/1961 (the text wrongly names Gizenga as the man shot); Hammarskjold died in the 17/09/1961 crash at Ndola; Katanga's secession ended 14/01/1963 and Kolwezi fell 21/01/1963; UN troops left 30/06/1964. Kouassi calls the UN a collective imperial power in the Congo as well as a partner; the cause of the crash remains unexplained.

Names Antoine Gizenga as the leader captured by Mobutu's troops and shot in Katanga on 17 January 1961; it was Patrice Lumumba who was killed on that date, while Gizenga survived. A slip in the volume.

column4: Chapter 29 and 30, Lagos Plan, Berg and population
column5: Kouassi says the Lagos Plan (04/1980) disagreed with the Berg Report of 1981, outward-looking cash-crop exports against inward-looking self-sufficiency, and that ECA and OAU rivalry (Adedeji and Kodjo) dogged the plan; Mazrui's last chapter gives black Africa's population growth as 2.5 per cent in 1960-70, 2.7 in 1970-80, 3.1 in 1980-86 and 3.2 by 1989, and argues colonial education gave skills of communication, not production. Kouassi's 1981 date contradicts chapter 21's 1979 for Berg.

Mazrui sums the volume: decade of conflict 1935-45, struggle against colonialism 1945-60, nation-building since; the gender and skills revolutions; Nigeria's anarchic privatisation under Shagari; Suez as a turning point. Context; not used.
